::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🎯 Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

-   Say what RNA-seq measures and what it does not
-   Choose between poly(A) selection and rRNA depletion for a given question
-   Explain why raw counts cannot be compared, and what each normalisation corrects
-   Explain why count data needs a negative binomial model rather than a t-test
-   Read a volcano plot and an MA plot, and say which is the better diagnostic
-   Distinguish ORA from GSEA and name the three commonest misuses of enrichment analysis
-   ⚠️ Recognize when a "differential expression" result is really a change in cell composition
:::

> 🤔 **Motivating question**
>
> Your knockout has a phenotype. RNA-seq returns 847 differentially expressed genes. Which of them mean anything?

![](images/clipboard-3691346398.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. What RNA-seq Measures 📏 {#w4-s1}

## 1) Steady-state abundance, not synthesis {#w4-s1-1}

RNA-seq counts the transcripts present **at the moment you lysed the sample**.

-   That number = the balance of two rates: **transcription** and **degradation**
-   ⚠️ The assay cannot separate them
-   → a gene whose transcription doubles and a gene whose mRNA half-life doubles look **identical**

If the distinction matters to your hypothesis, you need a different assay:

-   **Nascent transcription** — GRO-seq, TT-seq
-   **Metabolic labelling** — SLAM-seq
-   **Translation** — ribosome profiling

## 2) ⚠️ RNA is not protein {#w4-s1-2}

-   Transcript and protein abundance correlate at **r ≈ 0.4** across genes
-   A real correlation — and nowhere near enough to treat mRNA as a proxy for protein for any individual gene

Missing from RNA-seq: translation efficiency, protein half-life, post-translational regulation. 🔗 W6 takes this up properly.

## 3) A snapshot, of a mixture {#w4-s1-3}

Two further limits, worth stating early:

-   ⚠️ **One time point** — transcriptional responses are dynamic. A single harvest can miss an effect entirely, or catch a transient one and misread it as steady state
-   ⚠️ **A mixture of cells** — bulk RNA-seq averages over every cell in the tube. [§7.2](#w4-s7-2) shows how badly that misleads; 🔗 W5 is the response

![The bench workflow. Every decision on this line constrains what the analysis can do.](/assets/img/w4/rnaseq_workflow.png){fig-align="center"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Experimental Choices That Change Your Results ⚙️ {#w4-s2}

## 1) Poly(A) selection vs. rRNA depletion {#w4-s2-1}

Ribosomal RNA = \~80–90% of total RNA in a cell. Sequence total RNA directly → most of your budget buys rRNA. Every protocol removes it, one of two ways.

![Where the reads go, and how to choose.](/assets/img/w4/library_selection.png){fig-align="center"}

-   **Poly(A) selection** — oligo-dT beads capture transcripts with a poly(A) tail. Clean, cheap, the default for DE studies
-   **rRNA depletion** — complementary probes remove rRNA, keep everything else: non-polyadenylated transcripts, nascent unspliced RNA, degraded fragments

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Which to choose

-   Standard mRNA DE, good-quality RNA → **poly(A)**
-   FFPE or degraded RNA → **rRNA depletion**. Poly(A) selection fails, because degraded transcripts have lost their tails
-   lncRNA, circRNA, histone mRNAs, nascent transcription → **rRNA depletion**

⚠️ Made at the bench. **Cannot be undone in analysis.**
:::

## 2) Stranded vs. unstranded {#w4-s2-2}

-   A stranded protocol records which strand the original transcript came from
-   \~10–20% of the genome has overlapping transcription on both strands → without strand information those reads are assigned ambiguously or wrongly
-   → **stranded is now standard**, and there is little reason not to use it

## 3) Read length, depth, and paired-end {#w4-s2-3}

| Choice | When it matters |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Longer reads** (2×150 vs 1×50) | Isoform and splice junction work; less benefit for plain gene-level counting |
| **Paired-end** | Isoforms, fusion detection, novel transcripts. For gene-level DE, single-end is often sufficient |
| **Depth** | See [§5.4](#w4-s5-4) — saturates much earlier than people expect |

## 4) Biological vs. technical replicates {#w4-s2-4}

-   **Technical replicate** — the same RNA sequenced twice
-   **Biological replicate** — a different animal, patient, or independently cultured dish

⚠️ Technical variability in RNA-seq is small; biological variability is not.

-   Sequencing one sample twice tells you almost nothing new
-   → **n counts biological replicates only**
-   Three flasks from the same passage split on the same day are closer to technical than biological, whatever the methods section calls them

## 5) ✅ Design checklist {#w4-s2-5}

Before samples leave the bench (🔗 [W1 §5.3](w1_intro.qmd#w1-s5-3)):

-   ✅ **Randomise across batches** — extraction day, library prep batch, sequencing run. All cases in batch 1 and all controls in batch 2 → unrecoverable
-   ✅ **Record RIN** and treat it as a covariate. RNA quality shifts measurements systematically
-   ✅ **Record everything else** you might need to adjust for — age, sex, tissue site, time of collection
-   ✅ **Decide n before you start** ([§5.4](#w4-s5-4))
-   ✅ **Keep the design balanced** — unbalanced designs are analysable but lose power fast

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. From Reads to Counts 🔢 {#w4-s3}

## 1) Spliced alignment {#w4-s3-1}

**The problem** — reads come from mature mRNA, but you align to a genome. A read crossing an exon–exon junction will not align contiguously.

**The fix** — spliced aligners (STAR, HISAT2) allow large gaps at annotated or novel junctions.

Use this route when read **position** matters: novel transcripts, splicing, fusions, allele-specific expression, or anything you want to view in a genome browser.

## 2) Pseudo-alignment {#w4-s3-2}

**Salmon** and **kallisto** skip base-level alignment. They ask only which transcripts a read is *compatible with*, then resolve the assignment statistically across all reads.

-   ✅ \~an order of magnitude faster, far less memory
-   ✅ transcript-level estimates at least as accurate for quantification
-   ❌ no BAM file → cannot inspect alignments
-   ❌ can only quantify transcripts already in the annotation

## 3) Gene level vs. transcript level {#w4-s3-3}

-   Most genes produce several isoforms
-   Transcript-level quantification → more informative, but noisier: reads shared between isoforms must be probabilistically assigned

💡 **The pragmatic standard** — quantify at transcript level, then **sum to gene level** (the `tximport` route). Gene-level results are more robust, and you keep the option of looking at isoforms later.

## 4) Multi-mapping reads {#w4-s3-4}

Reads mapping equally well to several places — paralogues, repeats, pseudogenes — must be handled somehow:

-   **Discard** → systematically under-counts gene families
-   **Distribute probabilistically** → better, but introduces its own uncertainty

⚠️ One of the invisible decisions baked into any count matrix you download from GEO (🔗 [W1 §2.2④](w1_intro.qmd#w1-s2-2-4)).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Normalization ⚖️ {#w4-s4}

## 1) Why raw counts cannot be compared {#w4-s4-1}

A count depends on three things that have nothing to do with biology:

1.  **Library size (depth)** — sequence twice as deeply → every gene doubles
2.  **Gene length** — a 10 kb transcript generates more fragments than a 1 kb transcript at the same molar concentration
3.  **Library composition** — the subtle one

![① and ② are the obvious problem. ③ is the one that motivates TMM and RLE.](/assets/img/w4/normalization.png){fig-align="center"}

## 2) ⚠️ The composition effect {#w4-s4-2}

**Sequencing measures proportions, not absolute amounts.** The total is fixed by how many reads you bought.

-   One gene — or a handful — becomes enormously abundant in one condition
-   → it consumes a larger share of the library
-   → **every other gene's proportion falls, though nothing happened to it**
-   ⚠️ Simple depth normalisation (CPM) cannot fix this, because depth is not what changed

**The fix** — TMM (edgeR) and RLE / median-of-ratios (DESeq2) both assume most genes are *not* differentially expressed, and use that majority to estimate a per-sample scaling factor.

→ why they are the standard for differential expression and CPM is not.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## The assumption behind TMM and RLE

Both assume **the majority of genes do not change**. Usually safe.

**Fails when there is a global transcriptional shift:**

-   MYC amplification
-   global transcriptional shutdown
-   some drug treatments
-   comparing very different tissues

→ in those cases you need spike-in controls (ERCC) to anchor the scale.
:::

## 3) Which measure, when {#w4-s4-3}

| Method | Corrects | Comparable | Use for |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Raw counts** | nothing | — | **Input to DESeq2 / edgeR** — do not pre-normalise |
| **CPM** | depth | between samples | Filtering low-expression genes |
| **RPKM / FPKM** | depth + length | within a sample only | Legacy; avoid for comparisons |
| **TPM** | depth + length | within and (loosely) between | Reporting expression levels, heatmaps |
| **TMM / RLE** | depth + **composition** | between samples | **Differential expression — the standard** |

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Never feed normalised values into DESeq2 or edgeR

-   These tools model **raw counts** and estimate their own size factors internally
-   Handing them TPM or CPM breaks the variance model
-   → invalidates the p-values

A common and quiet error.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5. Differential Expression 📊 {#w4-s5}

## 1) Why counts need a negative binomial model {#w4-s5-1}

-   **Pure random sampling** → counts would be **Poisson**: variance = mean. Technical replicates roughly behave this way
-   **Biological replicates** → far more variable. **Overdispersed**, and the excess variance grows with expression level

![Left: the reason a t-test on counts produces false positives. Right: the reason n = 3 works at all.](/assets/img/w4/mean_variance.png){fig-align="center"}

The **negative binomial** adds a dispersion parameter φ:

$$
\text{Var}(Y) = \mu + \phi \mu^2
$$

-   φ = 0 → recovers Poisson
-   Estimating φ honestly is what separates a valid analysis from an optimistic one

## 2) Dispersion, shrinkage, and why n = 3 works at all {#w4-s5-2}

**The problem** — three numbers give a terrible variance estimate. You cannot estimate a gene's variance from n = 3.

**The solution — borrow information across genes:**

-   fit a smooth trend of dispersion vs. mean expression using **all** genes
-   shrink each gene's noisy individual estimate toward that trend

💡 The single most important methodological idea in bulk RNA-seq, and why the standard tools outperform a per-gene t-test so decisively at small n.

## 3) The three standard tools {#w4-s5-3}

| Tool | Model | Notes |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **DESeq2** | Negative binomial; shrinkage of dispersion *and* log fold change | Conservative; good default; handles small n well |
| **edgeR** | Negative binomial; empirical Bayes dispersion | Very similar in practice; quasi-likelihood mode slightly more conservative |
| **limma-voom** | Transforms counts, models precision weights, then linear models | Fastest at large n; most flexible for complex designs |

💡 In benchmark after benchmark the three agree on large-effect genes and disagree at the margins.

→ **If your conclusion depends on which one you used, you do not have a conclusion.**

## 4) ⚠️ Sample size — the weakest link {#w4-s5-4}

![Left: power against replicates. Right: what extra sequencing depth actually buys you.](/assets/img/w4/power_replicates.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## n = 3 is a convention, not a justification

Three replicates detect only large, consistent changes. For human tissue with real between-individual variability, usually insufficient.

Rough orientation:

-   **Cell lines, clean perturbation** — n = 3–4 may be acceptable
-   **Mouse tissue** — n = 5–8
-   **Human tissue / clinical samples** — n = 10–20 minimum, more if the phenotype is heterogeneous

And note the right-hand panel: **depth saturates, replicates do not.**

-   20–30 M reads per sample is enough for most DE questions
-   → money spent beyond that would buy more power as **additional samples**
:::

## 5) Reading a results table {#w4-s5-5}

![Two views of the same result. Most papers show only the first.](/assets/img/w4/volcano_ma.png){fig-align="center"}

-   **Adjusted p-value** — almost always Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (🔗 [W1 §4.2](w1_intro.qmd#w1-s4-2)). "FDR \< 0.05" → \~5% of the genes on this list are expected to be false
-   **log₂ fold change** — 1 = a doubling, −1 = a halving. For small n, report DESeq2's **shrunken** LFC; raw LFCs at low counts are wildly unstable
-   **Volcano plot** — significance vs. effect size. ⚠️ Both threshold lines are conventions
-   **MA plot** — effect size vs. expression level. **The better diagnostic** — it reveals whether your hits are concentrated at low counts, which is what a poorly controlled analysis looks like

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Two habits worth breaking

**① Filtering by fold change alone.**

-   log₂FC = 3 with padj = 0.4 is not a finding
-   → fold-change thresholds without significance filtering are how "top 20 gene" lists become unreproducible

**② Treating the threshold as biology.**

-   padj = 0.049 and padj = 0.051 are indistinguishable
-   → report the ranked list, not just the cut
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 6. Making Biological Sense of a Gene List 🧠 {#w4-s6}

You now have 847 genes. A list is not a result — **what do they have in common?**

## 1) ORA vs. GSEA {#w4-s6-1}

![Two ways to ask the same question. They are not equivalent.](/assets/img/w4/ora_vs_gsea.png){fig-align="center"}

-   **ORA** (over-representation analysis) — take the significant gene list, ask by Fisher's exact test whether a pathway is over-represented relative to a background set
-   **GSEA** — take *all* genes ranked by some statistic, ask whether a pathway's members cluster toward one end. **No threshold applied**

💡 **GSEA's specific advantage** — it detects a pathway where fifty genes each shift by 1.3×. Coordinated, biologically meaningful, and **completely invisible to any threshold-based method**.

## 2) Which databases {#w4-s6-2}

| Resource | Content | Caution |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **GO** | Biological process, molecular function, cellular component | Highly redundant; terms nested at wildly different specificity |
| **KEGG** | Curated metabolic and signalling pathways | Manually curated but slow to update |
| **Reactome** | Detailed, hierarchical reaction-level pathways | Deeper than KEGG, more complex to summarise |
| **MSigDB Hallmark** | 50 refined, non-redundant gene sets | 💡 The best starting point — designed to reduce redundancy |

## 3) ⚠️ The three commonest misuses {#w4-s6-3}

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Enrichment analysis is easy to do and easy to do wrong

**① The wrong background set.**

-   Only 12,000 of 20,000 genes expressed in your tissue → your background is **12,000**
-   Using the full annotation inflates every p-value in the output
-   → the single most common error in the literature

**② Threshold sensitivity.**

-   padj 0.05 → 0.10 can change the top pathway entirely
-   → if your headline result does not survive that, say so

**③ Enrichment is not mechanism.**

-   "Enriched for immune response" describes your gene list. It identifies no driver, no direction, no cause
-   ⚠️ Large generic categories (immune, metabolic, cell cycle) are enriched in almost every perturbation, because they contain thousands of genes
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 7. Beyond Differential Expression 🌐 {#w4-s7}

## 1) Co-expression networks {#w4-s7-1}

Instead of comparing conditions → ask which genes vary *together* across samples.

-   **WGCNA** clusters genes into modules of correlated expression, then relates module summaries to traits
-   ✅ Useful when there is no clean two-group comparison, and to reduce 20,000 genes to a dozen interpretable modules
-   ⚠️ Needs many samples — 20 is a floor, 50+ is better. It is estimating a correlation structure

## 2) ⚠️ Deconvolution — the composition problem again {#w4-s7-2}

![The same logic as W3's cell composition confounder, in a different assay.](/assets/img/w4/deconvolution.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## "Neuronal genes down, microglial genes up"

Bulk expression = the **weighted average** of the cell types present.

-   Disease changes the mixture — neuron loss, immune infiltration, fibrosis
-   → coherent, highly significant "differential expression"
-   → **without a single cell changing what it transcribes**

🔗 Exactly the confounder from [W3 §5.3②](w3_epigenomics.qmd#w3-s5-3-2), in a different assay — and why so many bulk tissue studies report cell-type marker genes as their top hits.

**What to do:**

-   ✅ Estimate cell type proportions computationally (CIBERSORTx, MuSiC, BayesPrism — all need a single-cell reference) → include as covariates
-   ✅ Or measure single cells directly (🔗 W5)
:::

## 3) Splicing and isoforms {#w4-s7-3}

-   **Differential expression** — did the gene's total output change?
-   **Differential splicing** — did the *proportions* of its isoforms change?

The second can matter enormously with no change in the first.

Tools: DEXSeq (exon usage), rMATS and LeafCutter (splicing events).

⚠️ All need more depth and more replicates than gene-level DE. Paired-end reads help substantially.

## 4) Expression as a genetic trait {#w4-s7-4}

Bring W2 back.

-   **eQTL** — a genetic variant associated with a gene's expression level
-   **GTEx** — eQTLs across 54 human tissues from hundreds of donors

→ the main bridge from a non-coding GWAS hit to a candidate gene (🔗 [W2 §4.4](w2_genomics.qmd#w2-s4-4)).

⚠️ With a caveat that connects all three chapters so far: **eQTLs are tissue- and cell-type-specific.** An eQTL measured in whole blood tells you little about what a variant does in neurons.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 📝 Summary

-   RNA-seq measures steady-state abundance, in a mixture of cells, at one moment — not synthesis rate, not protein, not any single cell
-   Poly(A) selection is the default; rRNA depletion is required for FFPE, non-coding RNA, and nascent transcription
-   Pseudo-alignment is fast and accurate for quantification; spliced alignment is needed when read position matters
-   Raw counts are biased by depth, gene length, and **composition**. TMM and RLE correct composition → the standard for DE
-   ⚠️ **Never feed normalised values into DESeq2 or edgeR**
-   Counts are overdispersed → a negative binomial model is required. Shrinkage across genes is what makes small-n analysis possible
-   ⚠️ n = 3 is a convention. Depth saturates around 20–30 M reads; replicates do not saturate
-   The **MA plot** is a better diagnostic than the volcano plot
-   GSEA uses the whole ranked list; ORA throws it away. ⚠️ Wrong background sets are the commonest error in enrichment analysis
-   ⚠️ Bulk expression differences are frequently **composition** differences. Deconvolve, or go single-cell

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🔑 Key terms

| Term               | One-line meaning                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Poly(A) selection  | Capturing polyadenylated transcripts with oligo-dT     |
| rRNA depletion     | Removing ribosomal RNA with probes                     |
| Stranded library   | Records which strand a transcript came from            |
| Spliced alignment  | Alignment allowing exon–exon junction gaps             |
| Pseudo-alignment   | Transcript compatibility without base-level alignment  |
| Count matrix       | Genes × samples table of read counts                   |
| Library size       | Total reads for a sample                               |
| Composition effect | One gene's rise lowering every other proportion        |
| CPM / TPM / FPKM   | Depth- and length-normalised expression units          |
| TMM / RLE          | Composition-aware size factors (edgeR / DESeq2)        |
| Overdispersion     | Variance exceeding the Poisson expectation             |
| Dispersion (φ)     | The extra-Poisson variance parameter                   |
| Shrinkage          | Pulling noisy per-gene estimates toward a global trend |
| log₂ fold change   | Effect size on a log scale                             |
| Volcano / MA plot  | Significance vs. effect / effect vs. expression        |
| ORA                | Fisher test on a thresholded gene list                 |
| GSEA               | Enrichment across a full ranked list                   |
| WGCNA              | Clustering genes into co-expression modules            |
| Deconvolution      | Estimating cell type proportions from bulk data        |
| eQTL               | Variant associated with a gene's expression            |
